title: Hasan al-Basri
hookLine: the preacher of Basra who warned rulers and taught inner watchfulness

lines: A CIRCLE IN THE MOSQUE AT BASRA.
A MAN WHO SEEMED TO GRIEVE.
cards: Basra, a city in southern Iraq. In its mosque, an old man sits with a circle of listeners around him. He is not a ruler or a general.
He holds no office. The biographers describe him as a man who seemed always to be grieving, as if he had just come back from burying someone.
When he speaks about death and the day of reckoning, people lean in, and some weep with him. Yet this quiet, sorrowful man would say hard things about a feared governor of his day.
His name was al-Hasan, and because of the city, history calls him Hasan al-Basri. Today: the preacher who watched his own heart first.

teach.b: His world was the Umayyad world of new cities, new wealth, new palaces. Iraq was governed by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, a man the histories remember for his harshness.
The reports say Hasan spoke against al-Hajjaj's cruelty, and at times had to hide from him.
He didn't lead a revolt. When some urged him to join an armed rising, the reports say he refused. His fight was a different one.
Hasan kept turning his listeners back toward their own hearts.

One saying attributed to him runs something like this: son of Adam, you are nothing but days, and when a day goes, a part of you goes with it. Another says the believer is the one who holds himself to account.
Later Muslim writers developed that idea into disciplines of the inner life: muhasaba, taking account of yourself, and muraqaba, watchfulness, living as one who is watched by God.

They found its ground in the Qur'an, where God says He knows what a person's soul whispers, and is nearer to him than his jugular vein. For them, if God is that near, every thought is lived in company.
Sufi writers count Hasan among their early teachers, and scholars of law and doctrine claim him too.
A story told about the beginnings of the Mu'tazila school of theology even says it began when a student named Wasil ibn Ata left Hasan's circle over a disputed question.
Many streams, the story suggests, flowed from one mosque in Basra.

how: Some Muslims practice muhasaba, taking stock of the day's words and deeds, for example at night before sleep, and Sufi teachers describe muraqaba, watchfulness, as a discipline of the heart.

games.q: you're Hasan. people furious at the governor ask you to back an armed rising. what do you do?
o: join them and lead the fight.
refuse to take up arms, but keep speaking hard truths.
go silent and say nothing about the governor.
games.why: the reports say he refused the rising, yet he kept criticizing al-Hajjaj's cruelty and at times had to hide.

practice: Without changing anything, notice what is moving in you right now, a worry, a wish, a small irritation from this morning, and name each one quietly as it passes, the way someone on a riverbank might name the boats.
Don't chase them and don't scold them; just watch. If you pray, you can remember that, in Hasan's tradition, you are not the only one watching.

wordCard.voice: Hasan al-Basri. The preacher of Basra who spoke against a harsh governor, refused to take up arms, and taught people to hold themselves to account. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: watchfulness, living as one watched by God; a key word in the inner life Hasan taught.

carryVoice: Your line: watch the heart. You are nothing but days, so each one counts. That's day nine hundred eight.
